Imagine an army marching toward unknown, possibly dangerous territory. Not everyone marches at the same position. A small, brave group goes first — ahead of the main force. They face what's coming before anyone else does. They take the risks. They set the path. This front group is called the vanguard.

That is the heart of the word. The vanguard is whoever or whatever is at the front, leading the way into new or challenging ground.
Two Ways the Word Is Used

1. The Literal (Military) Meaning

In its original, concrete sense, the vanguard is the front section of an advancing military force — the soldiers who lead the march and are first to meet the enemy or enter new territory. Behind them comes the main body of troops, and behind that, the rear guard.

Think of it like a spear. The vanguard is the sharp tip that goes in first.

2. The Figurative (Everyday) Meaning — Far More Common

Today, most people use "vanguard" outside of military contexts entirely. In everyday language, the vanguard refers to the people, group, or ideas that are at the leading edge of any movement, field, or change — whether in science, art, politics, technology, culture, or society.

Whoever is pushing boundaries, exploring new ideas, and moving ahead of everyone else while the rest of the world catches up — that is the vanguard.

This figurative use follows the exact same logic as the military one. There's still a "front." There's still risk. There's still a group leading the way while others follow later.

This is important, because the word carries meaning beyond just "being first." When someone or something is described as being in the vanguard, it implies several things at once:

  • They are pioneers. They are doing something before the mainstream accepts or even understands it.
  • They are taking risks. The front is exposed. The vanguard faces obstacles, criticism, or uncertainty that those who follow them will not.
  • They are setting the direction. Others will follow in their path. The vanguard does not follow trends — it creates them.
  • They are ahead of their time. What the vanguard does today, the wider world will do tomorrow.

So the word is not just descriptive — it carries a sense of courage, vision, and leadership through action.
How It Is Typically Used in a Sentence

The most natural and common phrase is "in the vanguard of" or "at the vanguard of."

Here are clear examples:

  • "Marie Curie was in the vanguard of scientific research at a time when women were barely allowed into laboratories."
  • "That small company was in the vanguard of electric vehicle technology long before it became mainstream."
  • "The artists in Paris in the early 1900s were at the vanguard of modern painting — everyone else eventually followed."
  • "Civil rights activists were the vanguard of a social movement that changed the law of the land."
  • "This university has always been in the vanguard of climate science."

You can also use it as a standalone noun referring to the leading group itself:

  • "The vanguard pressed forward despite the resistance."
  • "She joined the vanguard of the movement in its earliest, hardest days."

"Vanguard" is almost always used with a positive or neutral connotation. Being in the vanguard is generally seen as admirable — it means someone is bold, visionary, and ahead of the crowd.

You would not normally say someone is "in the vanguard of corruption" or "in the vanguard of laziness." The word simply doesn't fit those contexts — it implies a kind of pioneering dignity. It's reserved for things worth leading.

These words are close in meaning but are not identical:

Pioneer — Very similar. A pioneer is someone who goes first and opens the way. The key difference: "pioneer" usually refers to an individual person, while "vanguard" more naturally refers to a group or the leading edge of a larger movement. You'd say "she was a pioneer," but "they were in the vanguard."

Trailblazer — Emphasizes the act of making a path where none existed. Slightly more informal than vanguard. A trailblazer cuts through the wilderness so others can follow.

Forerunner — A forerunner comes before something and signals or previews it, but doesn't necessarily lead it. A forerunner is more of a sign of what's coming; a vanguard drives what's coming.

Avant-garde — This is the artistic cousin of vanguard (they share the same origin). "Avant-garde" is used almost exclusively in art, music, film, and culture to describe experimental, unconventional work that is far ahead of mainstream taste.

Cutting edge — An informal phrase meaning the most advanced point of a field. "Cutting edge" describes a position in a field; "vanguard" describes the people or group occupying that position, and carries more of a sense of movement and leadership.

The vanguard, by definition, is temporary in its leading position. The whole point is that the rest of the world eventually catches up. What was once vanguard thinking eventually becomes mainstream. A vanguard group leads precisely because others are not yet there — once everyone arrives, there is no longer a vanguard, just a field.

This is why the word often carries a slightly historical or retrospective quality — we frequently look back and recognize who was in the vanguard of something: "They were in the vanguard of the digital revolution before most people had even heard of the internet."

Vanguard means the leading group — whether in a literal military march or in any field of human activity — the ones at the very front who take the risks, face the unknown first, set the direction, and pave the way for everyone else who will eventually follow.
